tier_reason: ketotek/crypto-bench is a 2013 third-party hobby harness with public code (crypto_bench.cpp, cryptopp.cpp, gcrypt.cpp, botan.cpp) and Makefile flags (-O2 -march=corei7-avx) but no compiler version, library versions beyond Botan 1.10, or CPU model, and only a README sample output; not A, not a well-known suite, so C.

corrections.caveats: Weak, old and third-party: a May 2013 hobby repository (2 stars, 8 commits, no licence shown) with a sample output only, no CPU model and no library versions except Botan 1.10 (from the Makefile). The 'MB/s' column is MiB/s (the driver divides by 1024 twice) and is timed with clock(), i.e. CPU time, over 50000 rounds of a 4096-byte buffer. The three library implementations are not like for like: Botan is called as a bare encrypt_n/decrypt_n block loop (ECB, no chaining mode) while Crypto++ and libgcrypt run CBC; every round of every library repeats object creation and key setup; libgcrypt handles are opened every round and never closed; Crypto++ goes through StringSource, StreamTransformationFilter and StringSink with heap allocation (the sample shows 412 MB of malloc traffic for encrypt). Crypto++'s encrypt_round builds its output string from the 4096-byte 'out' buffer with a strlen-style constructor and never copies the ciphertext back, so its decrypt pass decrypts an untouched buffer rather than a real round trip (the timed work is still 4096 bytes of CBC decryption). The Linux kernel AF_ALG path beat all three (135.10 and 315.98 MB/s). CAST-128 is a legacy cipher, and libgcrypt is not the category's usual baseline (OpenSSL), so the result says little about AES or SHA performance. Current independent data points the other way: https://github.com/scc-tw/cryptobench-cpp (Crypto++ 8.9.0 vs OpenSSL 3.6.0, result.json dated 2025-11-05 from a MacBook Air, CPU model not stated, median of 5 repetitions) has Crypto++ far behind OpenSSL, e.g. AES-128-GCM 54 vs 7880 MB/s and SHA-256 71 vs 2787 MB/s at 16 KiB, probably because ARM crypto instructions were not used (the same harness's Botan AES rows all failed, so treat it as a rough data point); and the 2014 gist https://gist.github.com/aalness/577c7a6da1e669a07db9 (no CPU or compiler stated) has Crypto++ SHA-256 slower than OpenSSL (286.192 ms vs 162.157 ms for 300000 32-byte hashes; 19195 ms vs 17554.8 ms at 8192 bytes), though about 2x faster than libsecp256k1's own SHA-256. The Crypto++ repository itself publishes no cross-library comparison (its README only lists benchmarks as a feature). License: the compilation is BSL-1.0 and individual files are placed in the public domain (some 32-bit ARM files are CRYPTOGAMS, BSD-style).

notes: README numbers match the record exactly (Crypto++ 101.73/109.73 vs libgcrypt 75.70/76.00 and Botan 96.69/97.17 MB/s); ratios recomputed. Shortcomings: off-baseline (libgcrypt CAST5, not OpenSSL), 2013 hobby harness with no CPU or versions, Botan run in ECB vs CBC, every round re-keys, and modern data shows Crypto++ slower than OpenSSL on AES-GCM and SHA-256. Metadata on github.com: 5.5k stars, last commit 2026-10-02 (active), latest version 8.9.0 (Oct 2023), BSL-1.0 compilation licence from License.txt.
